extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of advertising history, social historians, and readers interested in British gambling regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Historical account of regulatory, procedural, and operational rules governing 18th–19th century English state lotteries and associated insurance offices, emphasizing fraud-prevention measures, licensing requirements, record-keeping, and sanctions. Extracts rules/orders, legal findings, and parliamentary assessments used to evaluate or reform the lottery system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on tickets sold to one person
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent the monopoly of tickets in the State Lottery, it had been enacted that persons charged with the delivery of tickets should not sell more than twenty to one person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was intended to avoid concentration of tickets and upward pressure on prices; the provision was evaded by the use of pretended lists which defeated Parliament's object and injured public credit (example: 1754 oversubscription caused by fictitious lists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on receiving subscriptions before advertised day/time
rubrics_metrics.description: Receivers must not receive subscriptions before the day and hour advertised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recorded in the Leheup prosecution: receiving subscriptions early was one counted offence. The rule preserves fairness of access; evasion (e.g., pre-selling) led to legal action and was treated as a breach of trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on using fictitious names/lists to cover excess tickets
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers/receivers must not permit subscribers to use different or fictitious names to cover an excess of tickets (beyond statutory limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leheup was found guilty of permitting use of fictitious names to exceed the 20-ticket limit. Fictitious lists were a common evasion tactic and were explicitly condemned by parliamentary inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper disposition of bespoke or double-charged tickets
rubrics_metrics.description: Tickets which had been bespoke, not claimed, or were double charged should be returned to the managers, not disposed of privately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leheup was convicted for disposing of such tickets instead of returning them. Proper handling prevents fraud and improper enrichment by office-keepers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security checks on the boys who draw numbers (Order of 12 December 1775)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a boy is allowed to put his hand into either wheel, his bosom and sleeves must be closely buttoned, his pockets sewed up, and his hands examined; during duty he must keep his left hand in his girdle behind him and his right hand open with fingers extended; he must not leave the wheel without being examined by the nearest manager.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact original wording: '...be brought by the Proclaimer to the Managers on Duty, for them to see that the Bosoms and Sleeves of his Coat be closely buttoned, his Pockets sewed up, and his Hands examined; and that during the Time of his being on Duty, he shall keep his left Hand in his Girdle behind him, and his right Hand open with his Finders extended...' These procedural checks were directed at preventing concealment/returning of tickets and collusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manager oversight and random assignment of drawers (Plan of 16 January 1776)
rubrics_metrics.description: Have ten managers on the roll at Guildhall with two conveniently placed opposite the two boys at the wheels to observe strict conformity to rules; the twelve boys nominated should not be made known until the morning of drawing and the two boys sent to the wheels each day are to be chosen promiscuously from among the whole number without any regular course or order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to prevent bribery/corruption by ensuring close supervision and by making it impossible for any boy to know in advance when he will draw. The plan acknowledges extra expense but deems it necessary to prevent fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licence, security, and minimum share-size for lottery offices (statutory requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every office-keeper must pay for a licence and give tangible security not to infringe the Act; no smaller portion of any ticket than a sixteenth should be disposed of; all shares should be stamped at a designated office with original tickets kept at the office until after the drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: licensing and tangible security promote accountability; stamping of shares and retention of original tickets aims to reduce fraudulent subdivision and unauthorised dealing. Penalties accompany breaches (see separate penalties entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty for disposing of goods on lottery chances
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person disposing of goods or merchandise upon any chance relating to the drawing of any ticket is liable to a fine (statute specified a fine of £20 in the cited enactment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision sought to curb gambling-dealing in goods contingent on lottery outcomes as an evasion of share/restriction rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of insurance of tickets (Act of 1781 / later enforcement attempts)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Act was passed to prevent the insurance of tickets by any method; insuring tickets was made unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite the Act, office-keepers continued insuring and many prosecutions resulted. The text notes that profits often exceeded fines, so illegal insuring persisted; enforcement measures and further regulation attempted to curb the practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of early-number dissemination and centralized record-keeping (Commissioners' measures, 1793)
rubrics_metrics.description: No persons were to be suffered to take down numbers except the clerks of licensed offices known to the Commissioners; no slips were to be sent out; numbers were to be taken down by one clerk in one book; lists (e.g., Steel's) abolished and recompensed; magistrates to apprehend persons taking early numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim: prevent early leakage of drawn numbers which enabled insurance/insuring fraud. Centralized, single-book recording reduces opportunities for dissemination and collusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial sanctions and criminal liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations (e.g., permitting apprentices to insure, illegal insuring, fraudulent disposals) exposed offenders to civil damages, statutory penalties, fines, and imprisonment (examples: fines of £1,000 or £1,500; an order for £500 penalty plus three months' imprisonment in one case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The history shows variable enforcement and inconsistent recovery (e.g., some fined sums were contested in later proceedings); deterrence was undermined when profits of illegal activity exceeded likely sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative measures to prevent bribery of drawers (operational practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical measures included keeping the identities of the boys secret until the morning, employing extra attendants/managers, selecting boys promiscuously for wheel duty, and close observation of the boys during drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These operational precautions were explicitly recommended to prevent attempts 'to corrupt or bribe any of the Boys' as learned after discovered frauds; they trade extra expense for heightened integrity of the draw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary/social criteria for assessing lotteries (grounds for abolition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary reports (c.1807) declared that the Lottery was 'so radically vicious' that no regulatory system could remove its 'evils and calamities' — enumerated harms include increased idleness, dissipation, poverty, betrayal of trusts, destruction of domestic comfort, creation of madness, suicides, and crimes punishable by death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These societal harms were used as evaluative criteria by committees and witnesses (e.g., magistrates) to argue for suppression/abolition rather than further regulation of the State Lottery.
